Axes, points and the right-hand rule

PDF pages 2 and 3

On the board

Ch 12. Vectors & the Geometry of Space
12.1 3-D Coordinate Systems

Right-hand rule:

The board shows a right hand with the fingers curled and the thumb pointing up along zzz.

In the plane you need two numbers to say where a point is. In space you need three, so a third axis, the zzz-axis, is added through the origin at right angles to the other two. To reach P0(x0,y0,z0)P_0(x_0, y_0, z_0)P0​(x0​,y0​,z0​) start at the origin, move x0x_0x0​ along the xxx-axis, then y0y_0y0​ parallel to the yyy-axis, then z0z_0z0​ parallel to the zzz-axis. That is the blue path in the figure.

The right-hand rule fixes which way the zzz-axis points once xxx and yyy are drawn. Every sketch in this course uses that orientation: xxx coming toward you, yyy to the right, zzz up.

Projections onto the coordinate planes

PDF pages 2 and 3

On the board

(a,b,0)(a, b, 0)(a,b,0): the projection of P(a,b,c)P(a, b, c)P(a,b,c) onto the xyxyxy-plane (z=0)(z = 0)(z=0).

(a,0,c)(a, 0, c)(a,0,c): projection onto the xzxzxz-plane (y=0)(y = 0)(y=0).

(0,b,c)(0, b, c)(0,b,c): projection of P(a,b,c)P(a, b, c)P(a,b,c) onto the yzyzyz-plane (x=0)(x = 0)(x=0).

The three axes come in pairs, and each pair lies in a coordinate plane: the xyxyxy-plane is where z=0z = 0z=0, the xzxzxz-plane is where y=0y = 0y=0, and the yzyzyz-plane is where x=0x = 0x=0. To project PPP onto a coordinate plane, drop a perpendicular from PPP to that plane. The foot of the perpendicular keeps the two coordinates that live in the plane and sets the third to zero. The colours match the board: black for the xyxyxy-plane, red for the xzxzxz-plane, green for the yzyzyz-plane.

The same picture gives distances for free. P(a,b,c)P(a,b,c)P(a,b,c) is ∣c∣|c|∣c∣ from the xyxyxy-plane, ∣b∣|b|∣b∣ from the xzxzxz-plane and ∣a∣|a|∣a∣ from the yzyzyz-plane, because those are the lengths of the three dotted edges.

What a test question on this looks like

A point is given, say (3,4,6)(3, 4, 6)(3,4,6), and you are asked for its projection on each coordinate plane, usually with a sketch of the box that has the origin and the point as opposite corners and every corner labelled. The answers are (3,4,0)(3,4,0)(3,4,0) on the xyxyxy-plane, (3,0,6)(3,0,6)(3,0,6) on the xzxzxz-plane and (0,4,6)(0,4,6)(0,4,6) on the yzyzyz-plane, and the box is this figure with a=3a = 3a=3, b=4b = 4b=4, c=6c = 6c=6.

R3\mathbb{R}^3R3 and Euclidean 3-space

PDF pages 3 and 4

On the board

Defn:

R3=R×R×R={(x,y,z)∣x,y,z∈R}\mathbb{R}^3 = \mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R} = \{(x, y, z) \mid x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}\}R3=R×R×R={(x,y,z)∣x,y,z∈R}

Read “R-3”.

x,y,z∈Rx, y, z \in \mathbb{R}x,y,z∈R says: xxx, yyy, and zzz are members of the set of all real numbers.

The 1-1 correspondence between R3\mathbb{R}^3R3 and 3-d space is called 3-d rectangular coordinate system or Euclidean 3-space.

R3\mathbb{R}^3R3 is a set of number triples. Space is a set of geometric points. Once axes are chosen, every point gets exactly one triple and every triple names exactly one point. That matching is what “1-1 correspondence” means, and it is why we can move freely between an equation in x,y,zx, y, zx,y,z and a picture.

Curves in 2-D, surfaces in 3-D

PDF pages 4 and 5

On the board

In 2-d, the graph of an equation relating xxx and yyy, ex. 4x2+y=74x^2 + y = 74x2+y=7, is the set of points

{(x,y)∣4x2+y=7}\{(x, y) \mid 4x^2 + y = 7\}{(x,y)∣4x2+y=7}

Plotting the points draws a picture in 2-d:

4x2+y=74x^2 + y = 74x2+y=7 y=−4x2+7y = -4x^2 + 7y=−4x2+7

Set y=0y = 0y=0 for the xxx-intercepts:

0=−4x2+70 = -4x^2 + 70=−4x2+7 4x2=74x^2 = 74x2=7 x2=74x^2 = \tfrac{7}{4}x2=47​ x=±72x = \pm\frac{\sqrt 7}{2}x=±27​​

In 3-d, the graph of an equation relating x,y,zx, y, zx,y,z, ex.

4x2+y−6z=74x^2 + y - 6z = 74x2+y−6z=7

is the set of points

{(x,y,z)∣4x2+y−6z=7}\{(x, y, z) \mid 4x^2 + y - 6z = 7\}{(x,y,z)∣4x2+y−6z=7}

Plotting the points draws a picture in 3-d: a surface.

One equation removes one degree of freedom. In the plane you start with two (you may choose xxx and yyy), so one equation leaves a one-dimensional thing, a curve. In space you start with three, so one equation leaves a two-dimensional thing, a surface. Two equations at once in space leave a curve, which is what happens in example c below.

From your own notes on PDF page 4: “The point he's making”

EquationIn 2-D (R2\mathbb{R}^2R2)In 3-D (R3\mathbb{R}^3R3)
4x2+y=74x^2 + y = 74x2+y=7parabola (curve)parabolic cylinder (surface)
x=3x = 3x=3vertical lineplane
x2+y2=1x^2 + y^2 = 1x2+y2=1circlecircular cylinder

The table is the habit to build: the same equation means different things in R2\mathbb{R}^2R2 and R3\mathbb{R}^3R3. When a variable is missing from an equation in R3\mathbb{R}^3R3, that variable is free, so the 2-D picture gets copied along the missing variable's axis.

Slicing the surface at z=0,1,2z = 0, 1, 2z=0,1,2

PDF pages 1, 5 and 6

On the board

z=0z = 0z=0:

4x2+y−6(0)=74x^2 + y - 6(0) = 74x2+y−6(0)=7

z=1z = 1z=1:

4x2+y−6(1)=74x^2 + y - 6(1) = 74x2+y−6(1)=7 ⟺  4x2+y=13\Longleftrightarrow\; 4x^2 + y = 13⟺4x2+y=13 ⟺  y=−4x2+13\Longleftrightarrow\; y = -4x^2 + 13⟺y=−4x2+13

z=2z = 2z=2:

4x2+y−6(2)=74x^2 + y - 6(2) = 74x2+y−6(2)=7 ⟺  y=−4x2+19\Longleftrightarrow\; y = -4x^2 + 19⟺y=−4x2+19

Each slice is a parabola in the plane z=kz = kz=k opening toward negative yyy.

This is how to draw a surface you have never seen: hold one variable fixed and look at what is left. Fixing z=kz = kz=k cuts the surface with a horizontal plane, and the cut is a curve you already know. Here every cut is the parabola y=−4x2+(7+6k)y = -4x^2 + (7 + 6k)y=−4x2+(7+6k). It is the same parabola each time, pushed 6 units further along yyy for every 1 unit you go up. Stack those parabolas and you get the surface. The straight grey lines in the figure join matching points on the parabolas, and they show the surface is a parabolic cylinder that leans over.

What a test question on this looks like

You are given an equation in xxx, yyy, zzz and asked to describe and sketch the surface it represents in R3\mathbb{R}^3R3. Answer it the way the board does: set z=0z = 0z=0, z=1z = 1z=1, z=2z = 2z=2 (or whichever variable is easiest), name each slice, then say in words what the slices build.

What surface is it? Seven examples

PDF pages 7 to 12

On the board

Ex. What surface in R3\mathbb{R}^3R3 is given by:

a. x=4x = 4x=4

A plane parallel to the yyy-zzz plane.

Nothing is said about yyy or zzz, so they are free. Every point 4 units out along xxx qualifies, whatever its yyy and zzz.

b. y=−3y = -3y=−3

y=−3y = -3y=−3 is a plane parallel to the plane determined by the xxx- and zzz-axes.

Same idea with xxx and zzz free. The plane sits 3 units to the negative side of the xzxzxz-plane.

c. Points (x,y,z)(x, y, z)(x,y,z) with x2+y2=4x^2 + y^2 = 4x2+y2=4 and z=5z = 5z=5

Circle x2+y2=4x^2 + y^2 = 4x2+y2=4 on the plane z=5z = 5z=5.

Two conditions at once, so this is a curve and not a surface: the circle of radius 2 centred at (0,0,5)(0, 0, 5)(0,0,5), lifted 5 units above the xyxyxy-plane.

d. x2+y2=2x^2 + y^2 = 2x2+y2=2

x2+y2=2x^2 + y^2 = 2x2+y2=2 is a cylinder whose intersection with the plane z=k∈Rz = k \in \mathbb{R}z=k∈R is the circle with centre (0,0,k)(0, 0, k)(0,0,k) of radius 2\sqrt 22​.

In 2-space the equation is a circle. In 3-space zzz is missing, so the circle is repeated at every height. Slide the blue slice up and down: it never changes size.

e. {(x,y,z)∣x2+y2≤2,  1≤z≤5}\{(x, y, z) \mid x^2 + y^2 \le 2,\; 1 \le z \le 5\}{(x,y,z)∣x2+y2≤2,1≤z≤5}

Solid cylinder.

The inequality x2+y2≤2x^2 + y^2 \le 2x2+y2≤2 takes the inside of the cylinder as well as its wall. 1≤z≤51 \le z \le 51≤z≤5 keeps only the part between heights 1 and 5.

f. {(x,y,z)∣x2+z2≤2,  1≤y≤5}\{(x, y, z) \mid x^2 + z^2 \le 2,\; 1 \le y \le 5\}{(x,y,z)∣x2+z2≤2,1≤y≤5}

Solid cylinder of radius 2\sqrt 22​, centred about the yyy-axis.

This time yyy is the variable left out of the circle equation, so the cylinder runs along the yyy-axis, from y=1y = 1y=1 to y=5y = 5y=5.

g. y=2xy = 2xy=2x

A plane whose intersections with planes z=k∈Rz = k \in \mathbb{R}z=k∈R are lines y=2xy = 2xy=2x.

In 2-d this is a line through the origin. In 3-d, zzz is free, so the line is copied at every height and the copies make a vertical plane through the zzz-axis.

All seven come from one rule. Find the variable that does not appear. The surface is the 2-D graph of the equation, extended parallel to that variable's axis. An equals sign gives the wall only. An inequality fills it in.

What a test question on this looks like

A list of equations and inequalities such as x=5x = 5x=5, y≥0y \ge 0y≥0, x2+y2=4x^2 + y^2 = 4x2+y2=4 with z=−1z = -1z=−1, or x2+z2≤9x^2 + z^2 \le 9x2+z2≤9, and you describe in words the region of R3\mathbb{R}^3R3 each one represents. One sentence each, in the style of the board: name the object, then say where it sits (“a plane parallel to the yzyzyz-plane, 5 units in front of it”).

The distance formula

PDF pages 13 to 18

On the board

The distance formula (in 2-d):

d=(x2−x1)2+(y2−y1)2d = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}d=(x2​−x1​)2+(y2​−y1​)2​

The legs of the right triangle are x2−x1x_2 - x_1x2​−x1​ and y2−y1y_2 - y_1y2​−y1​, and ddd is the hypotenuse.

In 3-d:

Triangle in the plane z=z1z = z_1z=z1​:

k2=(x2−x1)2+(y2−y1)2k^2 = (x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2k2=(x2​−x1​)2+(y2​−y1​)2

Then the upright triangle PRQPRQPRQ:

d2=k2+(z2−z1)2d^2 = k^2 + (z_2 - z_1)^2d2=k2+(z2​−z1​)2 d2=(x2−x1)2+(y2−y1)2+(z2−z1)2d^2 = (x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2 + (z_2 - z_1)^2d2=(x2​−x1​)2+(y2​−y1​)2+(z2​−z1​)2

The distance formula (in 3-d):

d=(x2−x1)2+(y2−y1)2+(z2−z1)2d = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2 + (z_2 - z_1)^2}d=(x2​−x1​)2+(y2​−y1​)2+(z2​−z1​)2​

The 3-D formula is Pythagoras used twice. First on the floor of the box: the green triangle lies flat in the plane z=z1z = z_1z=z1​, its legs are the xxx- and yyy-differences, and its hypotenuse is kkk. Then standing up: the red triangle has kkk as one leg, the height difference z2−z1z_2 - z_1z2​−z1​ as the other, and the distance ddd as its hypotenuse. Substituting the first result into the second gives the formula. Turn the figure until you can see both right angles.

On the board

Ex. Find the distance between P(4,−3,7)P(4, -3, 7)P(4,−3,7) and Q(−1,6,2)Q(-1, 6, 2)Q(−1,6,2).

d=(−1−4)2+(6−(−3))2+(2−7)2d = \sqrt{(-1 - 4)^2 + (6 - (-3))^2 + (2 - 7)^2}d=(−1−4)2+(6−(−3))2+(2−7)2​ =25+81+25= \sqrt{25 + 81 + 25}=25+81+25​ =131= \sqrt{131}=131​

The order of subtraction does not matter because each difference is squared: (−5)2=52(-5)^2 = 5^2(−5)2=52. What does matter is the double negative in the middle term, 6−(−3)=96 - (-3) = 96−(−3)=9. 131\sqrt{131}131​ does not simplify (131131131 is prime), and it is about 11.4511.4511.45.

What a test question on this looks like

Three points PPP, QQQ, RRR are given and you find the side lengths of the triangle, then decide whether it is right-angled or isosceles. Compute ∣PQ∣|PQ|∣PQ∣, ∣QR∣|QR|∣QR∣, ∣RP∣|RP|∣RP∣ with the formula, then compare: two equal lengths means isosceles, and the squares of the two shorter ones adding to the square of the longest means a right angle.

The equation of a sphere

PDF pages 19 to 22

On the board

The equation of a sphere in R3\mathbb{R}^3R3 with centre C(h,k,l)C(h, k, l)C(h,k,l) of radius rrr:

(x0−h)2+(y0−k)2+(z0−l)2=r2(x_0 - h)^2 + (y_0 - k)^2 + (z_0 - l)^2 = r^2(x0​−h)2+(y0​−k)2+(z0​−l)2=r2

Every point on the sphere satisfies this equation, and every point of distance rrr from C(h,k,l)C(h, k, l)C(h,k,l) is on the sphere. So its equation is:

(x−h)2+(y−k)2+(z−l)2=r2(x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 + (z - l)^2 = r^2(x−h)2+(y−k)2+(z−l)2=r2

A sphere is the set of all points at one fixed distance rrr from a centre CCC. Take any point P(x0,y0,z0)P(x_0, y_0, z_0)P(x0​,y0​,z0​) on it and write “the distance from PPP to CCC is rrr” with the distance formula. Squaring both sides removes the square root and gives the first line. The argument runs both ways, which is the point of the sentence on the board: points on the sphere satisfy the equation, and points that satisfy the equation are on the sphere. Dropping the subscripts gives the equation of the whole sphere.

On the board

Ex. Find the equation of the sphere with centre C(2,5,−4)C(2, 5, -4)C(2,5,−4) containing the point P(4,8,1)P(4, 8, 1)P(4,8,1).

r2=(4−2)2+(8−5)2+(1−(−4))2r^2 = (4 - 2)^2 + (8 - 5)^2 + (1 - (-4))^2r2=(4−2)2+(8−5)2+(1−(−4))2 =4+9+25=38= 4 + 9 + 25 = 38=4+9+25=38 r=38r = \sqrt{38}r=38​

Eqn:

(x−2)2+(y−5)2+(z+4)2=38(x - 2)^2 + (y - 5)^2 + (z + 4)^2 = 38(x−2)2+(y−5)2+(z+4)2=38

The radius is not given, but a point on the sphere is, and the radius is the distance from the centre to that point. The equation needs r2r^2r2, so you can stop at 383838 and never take the square root. Watch the sign on zzz: the centre has l=−4l = -4l=−4, and z−(−4)z - (-4)z−(−4) is written z+4z + 4z+4.

What a test question on this looks like

You are given the centre of a sphere and one point it passes through, and you find its equation. Often there is a follow-up asking for its intersection with a coordinate plane such as the xyxyxy-plane, which you answer by setting z=0z = 0z=0 in your equation and reading off the circle that is left.

Completing the square to find a centre and radius

PDF pages 23 and 24

On the board

Ex. Find the centre and radius of the sphere

x2+y2+z2−4x+6y+4z+5=0.x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 4x + 6y + 4z + 5 = 0.x2+y2+z2−4x+6y+4z+5=0.

“Complete the square” for each of xxx, yyy, zzz:

x2−4x⏟(−42)2+y2+6y⏟(62)2+z2+4z⏟(42)2=−5\underbrace{x^2 - 4x}_{\htmlClass{k-green}{\left(\frac{-4}{2}\right)^2}} + \underbrace{y^2 + 6y}_{\htmlClass{k-green}{\left(\frac{6}{2}\right)^2}} + \underbrace{z^2 + 4z}_{\htmlClass{k-green}{\left(\frac{4}{2}\right)^2}} = -5(2−4​)2x2−4x​​+(26​)2y2+6y​​+(24​)2z2+4z​​=−5 x2−4x+4  +  y2+6y+9  +  z2+4z+4=−5+4+9+4x^2 - 4x + 4 \;+\; y^2 + 6y + 9 \;+\; z^2 + 4z + 4 = -5 + 4 + 9 + 4x2−4x+4+y2+6y+9+z2+4z+4=−5+4+9+4 (x−2)2+(y+3)2+(z+2)2=12(x - 2)^2 + (y + 3)^2 + (z + 2)^2 = 12(x−2)2+(y+3)2+(z+2)2=12

Centre: (2,−3,−2)(2, -3, -2)(2,−3,−2)

radius =12=23= \sqrt{12} = 2\sqrt 3=12​=23​

From your own notes on PDF page 23

Step 1. Group by variable, move the constant.

(x2−4x)+(y2+6y)+(z2+4z)=−5(x^2 - 4x) + (y^2 + 6y) + (z^2 + 4z) = -5(x2−4x)+(y2+6y)+(z2+4z)=−5

Step 2. Complete the square, three times. Each time: take half the linear coefficient, square it, add it to both sides.

x: half of −4-4−4 is −2-2−2, squared is 444
y: half of 666 is 333, squared is 999
z: half of 444 is 222, squared is 444

(x2−4x+4)+(y2+6y+9)+(z2+4z+4)=−5+4+9+4(x^2 - 4x + 4) + (y^2 + 6y + 9) + (z^2 + 4z + 4) = -5 + 4 + 9 + 4(x2−4x+4)+(y2+6y+9)+(z2+4z+4)=−5+4+9+4

Step 3. Factor.

(x−2)2+(y+3)2+(z+2)2=12(x - 2)^2 + (y + 3)^2 + (z + 2)^2 = 12(x−2)2+(y+3)2+(z+2)2=12

Answer. Centre: (2,−3,−2)(2, -3, -2)(2,−3,−2). Radius: r=12=23≈3.46r = \sqrt{12} = 2\sqrt 3 \approx 3.46r=12​=23​≈3.46.

The expanded equation hides the centre and radius. Completing the square puts it back into the form (x−h)2+(y−k)2+(z−l)2=r2(x-h)^2 + (y-k)^2 + (z-l)^2 = r^2(x−h)2+(y−k)2+(z−l)2=r2 so they can be read off. The green notes under the braces on the board are the numbers to add: half of each linear coefficient, squared. Whatever is added on the left must be added on the right, which is where −5+4+9+4=12-5 + 4 + 9 + 4 = 12−5+4+9+4=12 comes from. Read the centre with the signs flipped: (y+3)(y + 3)(y+3) means k=−3k = -3k=−3.

If the right-hand side had come out negative there would be no sphere at all, and if it came out zero the “sphere” would be a single point. A positive number, as here, is r2r^2r2.

What a test question on this looks like

An expanded equation such as x2+y2+z2+8x−6y+2z+17=0x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + 8x - 6y + 2z + 17 = 0x2+y2+z2+8x−6y+2z+17=0, and you show it is a sphere and find its centre and radius. Same three steps. If the squared terms have a common coefficient, such as 2x2+2y2+2z2=…2x^2 + 2y^2 + 2z^2 = \dots2x2+2y2+2z2=…, divide the whole equation by it first.
